Second Order Optimality Conditions

We test curvature of the Lagrangian, rather than the objective alone. Assume fff, gig_igi​ and hjh_jhj​ are C2C^2C2 near the point being tested. Use gi≤0g_i\le0gi​≤0, unrestricted equality multipliers, nonnegative inequality multipliers, and row Jacobians. The KKT reference owns the active/strong/weak definitions; the constraint-qualification reference owns feasible paths and tangent versus linearized cones. This page develops the second-order proofs and computational tests used in Lecture 21.

Helpful Cones¶

Linearized and critical directions¶

On open D⊂RnD\subset\mathbb R^nD⊂Rn, use C2^22 maps f:D→Rf:D\to\mathbb Rf:D→R, g:D→Rr\mathbf g:D\to\mathbb R^rg:D→Rr, h:D→Rm\mathbf h:D\to\mathbb R^mh:D→Rm. At a feasible KKT point (x∗,u∗,v∗)(\mathbf x^*,\mathbf u^*,\mathbf v^*)(x∗,u∗,v∗), write AI\mathcal A_IAI​ for active inequality indices, split into As\mathcal A_sAs​ (positive multiplier) and Aw\mathcal A_wAw​ (zero multiplier) for the chosen KKT vector. Combined active labels are tagged (h,j)(h,j)(h,j) and (g,i)(g,i)(g,i); equality 1 and inequality 1 are different constraints. With derivatives evaluated at the point,

C1={p:Jhp=0, Jg,AIp≤0},C_1=\{\mathbf p:\mathbf{J}_h\mathbf p=\mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{J}_{g,\mathcal A_I}\mathbf p\le\mathbf{0}\},C1​={p:Jh​p=0, Jg,AI​​p≤0},
(1)
C2={p:Jhp=0, Jg,Asp=0, Jg,Awp≤0}.C_2=\{\mathbf p:\mathbf{J}_h\mathbf p=\mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{J}_{g,\mathcal A_s}\mathbf p=\mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{J}_{g,\mathcal A_w}\mathbf p\le\mathbf{0}\}.C2​={p:Jh​p=0, Jg,As​​p=0, Jg,Aw​​p≤0}.
(2)

At a KKT point, C2=C1∩{∇fTp=0}C_2=C_1\cap\{\nabla f^T\mathbf p=0\}C2​=C1​∩{∇fTp=0}. Indeed stationarity gives ∇fTp=−∑i∈AIui∗∇giTp≥0\nabla f^T\mathbf p=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal A_I}u_i^*\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\ge0∇fTp=−∑i∈AI​​ui∗​∇giT​p≥0. Each term is nonnegative; equality to zero forces ∇giTp=0\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p=0∇giT​p=0 wherever ui∗>0u_i^*>0ui∗​>0. Weakly active inequalities retain their one-sided restrictions. Biegler (2010), p. 79; Nocedal and Wright (2006), (12.53), p. 330.

Under LICQ, C1C_1C1​ equals the tangent cone, including zero and arbitrary scales. Unit limiting directions are its unit section, as explained in the qualification reference. Neither C1C_1C1​ nor C2C_2C2​ need be a linear subspace.

Subspaces that bracket the critical cone¶

C3=ker⁡[JhJg,AI],C4=ker⁡[JhJg,As],C3⊆C2⊆C4.C_3=\ker\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{J}_h\\\mathbf{J}_{g,\mathcal A_I}\end{bmatrix},\qquad C_4=\ker\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{J}_h\\\mathbf{J}_{g,\mathcal A_s}\end{bmatrix},\qquad C_3\subseteq C_2\subseteq C_4.C3​=ker[Jh​Jg,AI​​​],C4​=ker[Jh​Jg,As​​​],C3​⊆C2​⊆C4​.
(3)

For g1=x1≤0g_1=x_1\le0g1​=x1​≤0, g2=x2≤0g_2=x_2\le0g2​=x2​≤0, f=−x1+x22f=-x_1+x_2^2f=−x1​+x22​, the origin has (u1,u2)=(1,0)(u_1,u_2)=(1,0)(u1​,u2​)=(1,0). The panels then show a quadrant (C1C_1C1​), a ray (C2C_2C2​), just zero (C3C_3C3​), and a line (C4C_4C4​). Holding more independent rows at equality makes a smaller subspace.

C3C_3C3​ is contained in C4C_4C4​. Under LICQ the column counts are n−rows⁡(A3)n-\operatorname{rows}(\mathbf{A}_3)n−rows(A3​) and n−rows⁡(A4)n-\operatorname{rows}(\mathbf{A}_4)n−rows(A4​); without full row rank use n−rank⁡(Ai)n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}_i)n−rank(Ai​). A nonempty weak set adds independent rows under LICQ, but strict complementarity makes the two row sets identical. Their null spaces coincide; separately computed bases need not be numerically identical.

Second Order Necessary Conditions¶

Complete necessary-condition proof¶

For C2C^2C2 data, a local minimum satisfying LICQ has unique KKT multipliers and obeys

pTWp≥0for every p∈C2,W=∇xx2L(x∗,u∗,v∗).\mathbf p^T \mathbf{W}\mathbf p\ge0\quad\text{for every }\mathbf p\in C_2, \qquad \mathbf{W}=\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2L(\mathbf x^*,\mathbf u^*,\mathbf v^*).pTWp≥0for every p∈C2​,W=∇xx2​L(x∗,u∗,v∗).
(4)

This is Biegler’s Theorem 4.17, p. 80 (apply the errata), and Nocedal–Wright’s Theorem 12.5, p. 332.

Complete proof. Fix p∈C2\mathbf p\in C_2p∈C2​. LICQ and the feasible-path construction give z(t)=x∗+tp+o(t)\mathbf z(t)=\mathbf x^*+t\mathbf p+o(t)z(t)=x∗+tp+o(t) with hj(z(t))=0h_j(\mathbf z(t))=0hj​(z(t))=0 and each active inequality exactly gi(z(t))=t∇giTp≤0g_i(\mathbf z(t))=t\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\le0gi​(z(t))=t∇giT​p≤0. A strongly active inequality has zero directional derivative; weakly active and inactive constraints have zero multiplier. Thus L(z(t),u∗,v∗)=f(z(t))L(\mathbf z(t),\mathbf u^*,\mathbf v^*)=f(\mathbf z(t))L(z(t),u∗,v∗)=f(z(t)) exactly. Stationarity eliminates the linear Taylor term, so

f(z(t))−f(x∗)=12t2pTWp+o(t2).f(\mathbf z(t))-f(\mathbf x^*)=\tfrac12t^2\mathbf p^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p+o(t^2).f(z(t))−f(x∗)=21​t2pTWp+o(t2).
(5)

A negative quadratic coefficient dominates the remainder for sufficiently small positive ttt and contradicts local minimality. This establishes the nonnegative curvature test.

The path correction is o(t)o(t)o(t); the second-order Taylor remainder is o(t2)o(t^2)o(t2). They are different quantities. The vanishing first derivative is what permits the o(t)o(t)o(t) displacement correction to leave the quadratic coefficient unchanged.

Second Order Sufficient Conditions¶

Complete sufficient-condition proof¶

For C2C^2C2 data at a KKT point, suppose

pTWp>0for every nonzero p∈C2.\mathbf p^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p>0\quad\text{for every nonzero }\mathbf p\in C_2.pTWp>0for every nonzero p∈C2​.
(6)

Then x∗\mathbf x^*x∗ is a strict local minimum. LICQ is not required for this sufficient test. Biegler, Theorem 4.18, pp. 81–82; Nocedal–Wright, Theorem 12.6, pp. 333–334.

Complete contradiction proof. If strict local minimality fails, choose distinct feasible zk→x∗\mathbf z^k\to\mathbf x^*zk→x∗ with f(zk)≤f(x∗)f(\mathbf z^k)\le f(\mathbf x^*)f(zk)≤f(x∗). Put rk=∥zk−x∗∥>0r_k=\|\mathbf z^k-\mathbf x^*\|>0rk​=∥zk−x∗∥>0 and pk=(zk−x∗)/rk\mathbf p_k=(\mathbf z^k-\mathbf x^*)/r_kpk​=(zk−x∗)/rk​. Compactness of the unit sphere gives a subsequence pk→p\mathbf p_k\to\mathbf ppk​→p with ∥p∥=1\|\mathbf p\|=1∥p∥=1. Constraint expansions give p∈C1\mathbf p\in C_1p∈C1​ without any CQ. Dividing the objective difference by rkr_krk​ gives ∇fTp≤0\nabla f^T\mathbf p\le0∇fTp≤0; stationarity gives ∇fTp≥0\nabla f^T\mathbf p\ge0∇fTp≥0, hence p∈C2\mathbf p\in C_2p∈C2​.

At every feasible point L(zk,u∗,v∗)≤f(zk)L(\mathbf z^k,\mathbf u^*,\mathbf v^*)\le f(\mathbf z^k)L(zk,u∗,v∗)≤f(zk) because u∗≥0\mathbf u^*\ge\mathbf{0}u∗≥0, g≤0g\le0g≤0 and h=0h=0h=0. Also L(x∗,u∗,v∗)=f(x∗)L(\mathbf x^*,\mathbf u^*,\mathbf v^*)=f(\mathbf x^*)L(x∗,u∗,v∗)=f(x∗). The stationary second-order expansion therefore yields

0≥L(zk)−L(x∗)rk2=12pkTWpk+o(1)⟶12pTWp>0,0\ge\frac{L(\mathbf z^k)-L(\mathbf x^*)}{r_k^2} =\tfrac12\mathbf p_k^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p_k+o(1) \longrightarrow\tfrac12\mathbf p^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p>0,0≥rk2​L(zk)−L(x∗)​=21​pkT​Wpk​+o(1)⟶21​pTWp>0,
(7)

a contradiction. This proof includes directions approaching the critical cone, rather than assuming a direction limit for every original sequence.

Does SOSC imply SONC? At a fixed multiplier vector, strict positivity implies nonnegativity on that same cone. But the necessary-condition theorem additionally assumes LICQ, whereas the sufficient-condition theorem does not. Do not transfer that hypothesis from one theorem to the other. In a degenerate problem different KKT vectors can give different Hessians and critical-cone descriptions; the fixed-vector sufficient test remains meaningful.

In Biegler’s second proof case, all positive-multiplier terms contribute to the first-order Lagrangian/objective difference. Keeping only one chosen negative contribution supports an inequality, not an equality unless the other terms vanish. The argument above keeps the full sum and avoids that omission.

Reduced Hessian¶

A basis for a linear null space¶

For a full-row-rank A∈Rm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n with m≤nm\le nm≤n, a null-space basis Z∈Rn×(n−m)\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}Z∈Rn×(n−m) has full column rank and AZ=0\mathbf{AZ}=\mathbf{0}AZ=0. Every vector in ker⁡A\ker \mathbf{A}kerA is uniquely Zq\mathbf{Z}\mathbf qZq. When m=nm=nm=n, the null space is {0}\{0\}{0} and Z\mathbf{Z}Z has zero columns; a curvature condition over its nonzero vectors is vacuous.

This is the row-oriented version of Biegler’s Definition 4.19, p. 82. If rows are dependent, the correct dimension is n−rank⁡An-\operatorname{rank}\mathbf{A}n−rankA, obtained with a rank-revealing factorization or SVD. Pivoting detects the dependence; it does not make dependent rows independent. An arbitrary critical cone cannot be represented by Zq\mathbf{Z}\mathbf qZq with unrestricted q\mathbf qq: that image is a subspace.

Complete QR construction and a small worked example¶

For independent rows, factor AT=Q[R;0]\mathbf{A}^T=\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{R};0]AT=Q[R;0], where Q=[QR QN]\mathbf{Q}=[\mathbf{Q}_R\ \mathbf{Q}_N]Q=[QR​ QN​] is n×nn\times nn×n orthogonal and R\mathbf{R}R is nonsingular m×mm\times mm×m upper triangular. Since QRTQN=0\mathbf{Q}_R^T\mathbf{Q}_N=\mathbf{0}QRT​QN​=0,

AQN=RTQRTQN=0,\mathbf{AQ}_N=\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{Q}_R^T\mathbf{Q}_N=\mathbf{0},AQN​=RTQRT​QN​=0,
(8)

and QN\mathbf{Q}_NQN​ has n−mn-mn−m independent columns, so it spans the null space. An economic QR can omit this complement; request the complete factorization. Biegler (4.58), p. 82; Nocedal–Wright (12.74), p. 337.

For A=[110011]\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]A=[10​11​01​], choose

QR=[1/2−1/61/21/602/6],Z=(−1,1,−1)T3,R=[21/203/2].\mathbf{Q}_R=\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt2&-1/\sqrt6\\1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt6\\0&2/\sqrt6\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{Z}=\frac{(-1,1,-1)^T}{\sqrt3},\quad \mathbf{R}=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\0&\sqrt{3/2}\end{bmatrix}.QR​=⎣⎡​1/2​1/2​0​−1/6​1/6​2/6​​⎦⎤​,Z=3​(−1,1,−1)T​,R=[2​0​1/2​3/2​​].
(9)

Check AT=QRR\mathbf{A}^T=\mathbf{Q}_R\mathbf{R}AT=QR​R, AZ=0\mathbf{AZ}=\mathbf{0}AZ=0 and ZTZ=1\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z}=1ZTZ=1. The two constraint planes intersect in the line spanned by Z\mathbf{Z}Z.

For numerical work use a stable library factorization, inspect the rank threshold, and check AZ\mathbf{AZ}AZ, the rank of Z\mathbf{Z}Z, and ZTZ\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z}ZTZ when an orthonormal basis is intended. Loss of orthogonality does not by itself prove that a full-rank, exactly null basis fails to span the null space. The Math-Primer D3 experiment illustrates orthogonality loss; its economic QR alone does not construct QN\mathbf{Q}_NQN​. Watkins (2002), Sections 3.2–3.3, provides the reflector/rotator background.

Reduced Hessian and basis invariance¶

For symmetric W\mathbf{W}W and p=Zq\mathbf p=\mathbf{Z}\mathbf qp=Zq,

pTWp=qT(ZTWZ)q.\mathbf p^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p=\mathbf q^T(\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ})\mathbf q.pTWp=qT(ZTWZ)q.
(10)

Because Z\mathbf{Z}Z is a full-rank basis for ker⁡A\ker \mathbf{A}kerA, nonzero q\mathbf qq and nonzero p\mathbf pp correspond. Thus curvature is positive (semi)definite on this subspace exactly when the reduced Hessian HR=ZTWZ\mathbf{H}_R=\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}HR​=ZTWZ is positive (semi)definite. A different basis Z~=ZT\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}=\mathbf{Z}\mathbf TZ=ZT, with TTT nonsingular, gives H~R=TTHRT\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_R=\mathbf T^T\mathbf{H}_R\mathbf THR​=TTHR​T. Definiteness and inertia are invariant; eigenvalue magnitudes generally change. Orthonormal bases make eigenvalue scales easier to interpret.

For f=x12−x22f=x_1^2-x_2^2f=x12​−x22​, h=x2=0h=x_2=0h=x2​=0, the origin has v=0v=0v=0, W=diag⁡(2,−2)\mathbf{W}=\operatorname{diag}(2,-2)W=diag(2,−2) and Z=(1,0)T\mathbf{Z}=(1,0)^TZ=(1,0)T. Its reduced Hessian is 2, so the origin is a strict constrained minimum despite an indefinite full Hessian.

Let Z3,Z4\mathbf{Z}_3,\mathbf{Z}_4Z3​,Z4​ span C3,C4C_3,C_4C3​,C4​. Under the necessary theorem’s hypotheses, Z3TWZ3⪰0\mathbf{Z}_3^T\mathbf{WZ}_3\succeq0Z3T​WZ3​⪰0 is a weaker necessary test because it checks fewer directions. At a KKT point, Z4TWZ4≻0\mathbf{Z}_4^T\mathbf{WZ}_4\succ0Z4T​WZ4​≻0 is a stronger sufficient test because it checks more directions than C2C_2C2​ requires. Neither is a general equivalence to the exact cone test.

For example, on x1,x2≥0x_1,x_2\ge0x1​,x2​≥0, the function f=12(x12+x22+4x1x2)f=\tfrac12(x_1^2+x_2^2+4x_1x_2)f=21​(x12​+x22​+4x1​x2​) has a strict minimum at the origin with zero multipliers. Its critical cone is the nonnegative quadrant. The Hessian [1221]\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right][12​21​] has eigenvalues 3 and −1, but pTWp=p12+p22+4p1p2>0\mathbf p^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf p=p_1^2+p_2^2+4p_1p_2>0pTWp=p12​+p22​+4p1​p2​>0 for every nonzero critical direction. The whole-space C4C_4C4​ test fails although the exact SOSC holds. Conversely, the all-active null space can be zero and its necessary test vacuous even at a nonminimum. Strict complementarity makes C2=C3=C4C_2=C_3=C_4C2​=C3​=C4​, so the subspace tests become exact. Biegler, pp. 82–83.

Example¶

Example 4.20: a positive one-dimensional reduced Hessian¶

Use the canonical positive-domain log model with g=4−x1x2≤0g=4-x_1x_2\le0g=4−x1​x2​≤0. Biegler’s Example 4.20 is on p. 83. Its solution is approximately (1.7981,2.2245)(1.7981,2.2245)(1.7981,2.2245) with u=0.5685>0u=0.5685>0u=0.5685>0, so strict complementarity holds. The corrected Lagrangian Hessian is

W=[2+1/x121−u1−u3+1/x22]≈[2.30930.43150.43153.2021].\mathbf{W}=\begin{bmatrix}2+1/x_1^2&1-u\\1-u&3+1/x_2^2\end{bmatrix} \approx\begin{bmatrix}2.3093&0.4315\\0.4315&3.2021\end{bmatrix}.W=[2+1/x12​1−u​1−u3+1/x22​​]≈[2.30930.4315​0.43153.2021​].
(11)

The gradient row is Jg=(−x2,−x1)\mathbf{J}_g=(-x_2,-x_1)Jg​=(−x2​,−x1​) and a unit tangent basis is approximately (−0.6286,0.7777)T(-0.6286,0.7777)^T(−0.6286,0.7777)T. The reduced Hessian is about 2.42736 using unrounded values; the errata’s 2.4272 uses the rounded printed basis. The printed 1.0331 and Hessian (4.66) need the errata. With the displayed +9 objective, f≈−0.4944f\approx-0.4944f≈−0.4944; the book’s −2.4944 is two lower, consistent with +7. The existing source correction explains the constant without changing the derivatives or minimizer.

The Biegler errata corrects p. 83’s Hessian and reduced-Hessian number. The native calculation below preserves the original rounded NumPy example, followed by the actual Pyomo solve and an analytic derivative/basis check. These are numerical evaluations of a supplied model, not a reason to reuse the uncorrected printed matrix.

Calculation with numpy¶

import numpy as np

# Define the Hessian of the Lagrange function
hessian_L = np.array([[2.3093, 0.4315], [0.4315, 3.2021]])
print(hessian_L)

Calculate the complete QR factorization.

A=Q×R\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \times \mathbf{R}A=Q×R
(12)
# Calculate the COMPLETE QR factorization
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A, mode="complete")

The code’s A stacks the single gradient as a column, so A = J_g.T. The second column of the complete Q\mathbf{Q}Q lies in ker⁡AT\ker \mathbf{A}^TkerAT, not ker⁡A\ker \mathbf{A}kerA. Indeed ATQN=RTQRTQN=0\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{Q}_N=\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{Q}_R^T\mathbf{Q}_N=\mathbf{0}ATQN​=RTQRT​QN​=0. Since QN\mathbf{Q}_NQN​ has the right number of independent columns, it is a basis for the tangent line. Now evaluate QNTWQN\mathbf{Q}_N^TWQ_NQNT​WQN​.

# Calculate the reduced Hessian
print("Reduced Hessian w.r.t. null space of constraints:")
Q[:, 1].T @ hessian_L @ Q[:, 1]

Calculate with Pyomo¶

Define and solve the model¶

import pyomo.environ as pyo

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

# Define variables
m.x1 = pyo.Var(initialize=1)
m.x2 = pyo.Var(initialize=1)

# Define constraints
# Note: changing this to an equality constraint
# changes the reduced_hessian
m.con1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=4 - m.x1 * m.x2 <= 0)

# Define objective
m.obj = pyo.Objective(
    expr=m.x1**2
    - 4 * m.x1
    + 1.5 * m.x2**2
    - 7 * m.x2
    + m.x1 * m.x2
    + 9
    - pyo.log(m.x1)
    - pyo.log(m.x2)
)

# Obtain dual solutions from first solve and send to warm start
m.dual = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT)

# Specify Ipopt as the solver and solve
opt = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
results = opt.solve(m, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)

Actual-point derivative and basis check¶

The model and solve above are unchanged. The following cell differentiates the actual Pyomo expressions and archives one shared basis-comparison figure. It records the point before the later experimental barrier calls solve the model again.

from pyomo.core.expr.calculus.derivatives import differentiate, Modes

variables = [m.x1, m.x2]
x_actual = np.array([pyo.value(v) for v in variables])
u_actual = -float(m.dual[m.con1])
g_expr = m.con1.body
gradient_actual = np.array(differentiate(m.obj.expr, wrt_list=variables))
jac_actual = np.array(differentiate(g_expr, wrt_list=variables)).reshape(1, 2)
lag_expr = m.obj.expr + u_actual * g_expr
lag_gradient = differentiate(lag_expr, wrt_list=variables, mode=Modes.reverse_symbolic)
W_actual = np.array([differentiate(e, wrt_list=variables) for e in lag_gradient])
Q_actual, _ = np.linalg.qr(jac_actual.T, mode="complete")
Z_actual = Q_actual[:, 1:]
bases = np.column_stack([Z_actual[:, 0], [1, -jac_actual[0, 0]/jac_actual[0, 1]],
                         [-jac_actual[0, 1]/jac_actual[0, 0], 1]])
reduced_values = np.einsum("ij,ik,kj->j", bases, W_actual, bases)
stationarity_actual = gradient_actual + jac_actual.T[:, 0] * u_actual
assert np.all(x_actual > 0) and u_actual > 0
assert np.linalg.norm(stationarity_actual, np.inf) < 1e-6
assert np.linalg.norm(jac_actual @ bases, np.inf) < 1e-12
assert np.all(reduced_values > 0)
print("Actual point:", x_actual, "canonical u:", u_actual)
print("Corrected Lagrangian Hessian:\n", W_actual)
print("Unit QR basis:", Z_actual[:, 0])
print("Reduced Hessians: unit QR, x1 parameter, x2 parameter:", reduced_values)
q_grid = np.linspace(-1, 1, 201)
x1_curve = np.linspace(x_actual[0] - .5, x_actual[0] + .5, 201)
soc_data = {"point": x_actual.tolist(), "objective": float(pyo.value(m.obj)),
            "u": u_actual, "J": jac_actual.tolist(), "W": W_actual.tolist(),
            "bases": bases.tolist(), "reduced_values": reduced_values.tolist(),
            "q": q_grid.tolist(), "quadratic_change": (.5*reduced_values[:,None]*q_grid[None,:]**2).tolist(),
            "curve_x1": x1_curve.tolist(), "curve_x2": (4/x1_curve).tolist()}
helper.save_results("soc-log-bases", soc_data, notebook="notebooks/7-dev/Second-Order.ipynb",
    source_cells=[("notebooks/7-dev/Second-Order.ipynb", "results:soc-log-model"),
                  ("notebooks/7-dev/Second-Order.ipynb", "results:soc-log-curvature")],
    description="Actual +9 log-model point, symbolic Lagrangian derivatives and three tangent parameter scales.",
    solver=str(opt), quiet=True)
results = soc_data

For this canonical upper inequality, the imported Pyomo suffix is negative and u=−m.dual[m.con1]u=-\texttt{m.dual[m.con1]}u=−m.dual[m.con1] gives the nonnegative canonical multiplier. The analytic stationarity check above verifies the mapping at the actual point. See the KKT suffix reference for other constraint orientations.

The original model comment about changing the inequality to an equality concerns the numerical barrier treatment. At the same point and matching multiplier, the exact active-tangent reduced Hessian is the same; changing a constraint’s role does not by itself change that quadratic form.

Extract the reduced Hessian¶

# Warning: this Pyomo feature is experimental

from pyomo.contrib.interior_point.inverse_reduced_hessian import (
    inv_reduced_hessian_barrier,
)

# https://github.com/Pyomo/pyomo/blob/main/pyomo/contrib/interior_point/inverse_reduced_hessian.py

Compute the reduced Hessian with respect to x1x_1x1​

solve_result, inv_red_hes = inv_reduced_hessian_barrier(
    m,
    independent_variables=[m.x1],  # Warning: these variables cannot be at their bounds
    tee=True,
)

print("\nReduced Hessian w.r.t. x1:")
print(np.linalg.inv(inv_red_hes))

Coordinate parameters are tangent bases, not coordinate-axis directions¶

At x1x2=4x_1x_2=4x1​x2​=4, the tangent basis for parameter x1x_1x1​ is Zx1=(1,−x2/x1)TZ_{x_1}=(1,-x_2/x_1)^TZx1​​=(1,−x2​/x1​)T, and for parameter x2x_2x2​ it is Zx2=(−x1/x2,1)TZ_{x_2}=(-x_1/x_2,1)^TZx2​​=(−x1​/x2​,1)T. Neither is the coordinate vector (1,0)T(1,0)^T(1,0)T or (0,1)T(0,1)^T(0,1)T. Each equals a nonzero scalar multiple of the unit QR basis; consequently its reduced Hessian scales by the square of that scalar. Positive definiteness survives, while the three numerical values differ.

The official experimental API documentation and the installed implementation show that inv_reduced_hessian_barrier solves the model again, forms a barrier-subproblem KKT matrix, and extracts an inverse-Hessian block for selected independent variables. At a finite barrier parameter this is not an exact critical-cone certificate. Its selected variables must be away from their bounds. Check solve status, evaluate the actual active-point derivatives, and distinguish coordinate scaling from finite-barrier and roundoff effects when comparing outputs.
